title: AI Boom Is Triggering ‘Dutch Disease’ In The US Economy, Warns Apollo’s Torsten Slok — ‘The Only Durable Fix Is…’
source_used: Stocktwits (read on the Yahoo Finance copy)
key_facts: Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in a note on Friday (9 Oct 2026) that the AI boom is absorbing capital, electricity and workers at a pace that could leave other parts of the economy struggling to compete for resources.
He called this a form of 'Dutch disease', in which a booming sector draws resources away from other areas.
Rate-sensitive parts of the economy, including housing and autos, face pressure from elevated interest rates while hyperscalers keep spending heavily.
Consensus estimates for AI capital spending in 2027 have kept rising, with no sign investors expect a slowdown.
He said this makes policy difficult for the Federal Reserve and could keep interest rates higher for longer, particularly with the fiscal boost from the One Big Beautiful Bill.
He said the only durable fix is expanding the supply of power, chips and infrastructure.

An earlier note of his said AI investment is accelerating about 0.85 percentage points of GDP a year, faster than the housing boom (about 0.5) or telecom cycle (about 0.15), and could unwind at a similar pace if demand disappoints.
quote_evidence: "Because monetary policy cannot resolve this sectoral imbalance, the only durable fix is expanding the supply of power, chips and infrastructure," he added.
Slok argued in a note on Friday that the rapid expansion of AI investment is creating an unusual economic imbalance, with resources increasingly flowing toward the sectors supporting the AI buildout.
This article was originally published on StockTwits.
why_it_matters_hint: An economist links the AI spending boom to rates staying higher for housing and car buyers.
event_date: Friday 9 Oct 2026 (Slok note); first reported Saturday 10 Oct 2026
